On
Ethiopia’s history has come back to haunt it.
Late last month, seven armed groups - among them the Fano militia in Amhara, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Oromo Liberation Army - announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, and vowed to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
Within days, Tigrayan forces had seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and opened fronts in Afar and Amhara. By 25 September, phone and internet lines in Tigray were cut. This time it was the TPLF, not Addis Ababa, that ordered the blackout.
Most commentary reads the new conflict as the collapse of the Pretoria agreement, a 2022 peace deal to end two years of war. But the story is much older than the Pretoria process and Abiy himself.
For nearly two centuries, Ethiopian politics has swung between a centre that wants to command, and regions that insist on ruling themselves. Each time the pendulum has pushed hard towards the centre, the peripheries have found a way to unite against it.
After the Zemane Mesafint (“Era of the Princes”) in the 18th and 19th centuries, when regional lords ran their own affairs, Tewodros II tried to rebuild the empire by the sword. The provinces revolted one after another, and in 1868, he died at Magdala, his army reduced to remnants.
Similarly, former emperor Haile Selassie’s 1962 dissolution of the Eritrean federation turned a small insurgency into a 30-year war. When I sat down with Mothin Ali early on Sunday, he was in an energetic mood.
It was the third and final day of what must have been an arduous Green Party conference for its co-deputy leader, who was dressed in his usual suit and flat cap.
"It's been a fantastic year," Ali beamed. "We had 400 councillors elected in May, 1,300 councillors in all, a fifth MP in parliament and our membership has quadrupled.
"It's a phenomenal record so far."
The Greens surged in the polls last year after Polanski was elected leader. They gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did.
Polanski is at least partially responsible for Keir Starmer's downfall and Andy Burnham's premiership. On Friday evening the renowned political analyst John Curtice argued as much at a packed fringe event.
The conference in the sunny seaside town of Brighton was full of energy. For many members it was the event of the year: Friends roved the conference in groups and went off to restaurants and bars in the evening. They were diverse in age and ethnicity; many wore keffiyehs and Palestine badges.
But as Curtice pointed out - turning smiles into frowns - the Greens now have their work cut out for them under a new and much more popular prime minister.
Polling shows support for the Greens has plummeted in the past few months.
Andy Burnham has taken steps to address key grievances that led Labour voters to switch to the Greens under Starmer.
So far, the most significant has been the Labour government's sanctions on Israeli settlements.

"My mother was thrown against the wall by the force of the explosion, and my grandmother was engulfed in flames after the missile hit the house," 14 year-old Fuad told Middle East Eye.

"The Israeli occupation does not distinguish between Christians and Muslims. We are all at risk of being killed in Gaza. I don’t know if I will still be alive after this interview."

As olive harvest nears, Palestinian farmers urgently need international protection: Opinion by Fareed Taamallah
Every October, the ancient olive groves in my hometown and across the occupied West Bank become dynamic hubs of life and labour. For generations of Palestinians, the olive harvest has been the pulse of our economic survival and a living link to our ancestors. The olive tree, resilient and deep-rooted, is a symbol of who we are and of our connection to this land.
As this year's harvest approaches, our villages are gripped by a dread I have not seen before. In recent weeks, the situation across the West Bank has deteriorated sharply. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, has said that the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is the "main focus" of truce talks with Washington.
Speaking at a news conference, Baghaei said that Tehran is "focusing on the strait foremost", and that its primary concern is "to reach a solution and to have peace and stability restored within this waterway". He added that, by contrast, Washington's strategy to end the conflict is focused on Iran's nuclear file.
He told reporters that the return of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors has not been discussed by Iran's leadership.
He noted that the peace process has been thwarted by the "volatility and fluctuation" of Washington's decision-making.
“This is reflected in their conflicting statements as well as their fluctuating demands. This is a problem faced not only by Iran, but by all the countries dealing with the United States. These countries are openly complaining about the crisis,” said Baghaei said.
Meanwhile, Tasnim news agency reports that Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a meeting with foreign ambassadors that there is "no military solution or any solution based on new sanctions" to the seven-month-long conflict.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Araghchi said.
He added that Tehran is “serious about finding diplomatic solutions, just as we are serious about defending ourselves”.

Hegseth: US blockade of Hormuz ironclad, Iran should make right choice
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said that the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is “ironclad” and that US President Donald Trump has “all the options he needs on the table” if Iran continues to “play games” with the strait, according to an AP report carried by the Times of Israel.
“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it, we do,” Hegseth told reporters.
“They have literally gotten nothing through. Our blockade has been ironclad and we’re running almost at prewar levels every single night through that, you see that as far as the throughput.”
He added: “So we feel like we’re in a very strong position. Iran ought make the right choice. If they don’t, the president is going to have all the options he needs on the table. But he is not going to let these things extend unnecessarily. He understands what the mission is and we can get it done when called upon.”
Hegseth also said that Trump is “hellbent” on Iran not having a nuclear weapon, the report said.
“The message is very simple: Iran will never ever ever have a nuclear weapon. President Trump is hell-bent and determined to ensure that they do not; they will not,” Hegseth said.

Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, has warned the United Arab Emirates (UAE) against challenging Tehran and its sovereignty over three islands in the Persian Gulf.
In a post on his X account, Velayati dismissed recent claims made by the UAE at the United Nations General Assembly regarding sovereignty over Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, and Abu Musa, saying the three islands will remain Iranian forever, according to IRNA.
"A country whose political life does not reach half a century makes claims from the UN podium about islands that have been recorded under Iran's name in historical documents and maps of past centuries," Velayati said in the Farsi-language post.
He added that the UAE should not "rely on foreign powers" for its security and should instead pursue good relations with its neighbours, IRNA reported.
"The neighbour stays, and the guest goes… Regional experience has shown that imported security has an expiration date," said the former Iranian foreign minister.

Six months into Israel's assault on Gaza in March 2024, when more than 120 Palestinians were being killed in air strikes each day, Broadway performer Allie Trimm was approached by the writer of a project she had just been fired from.
"You and I are not so different. We both don't want to see innocent people get hurt," the writer told her.
"We just have a different idea of who's innocent."
Trimm, an actress and singer since the age of nine, had become an advocate for Palestinian rights after images of children torn apart by US-supplied weapons flooded her social media feeds, as they had for countless other Americans since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
Just under 1,200 people - Israelis and foreign nationals - were killed that morning, including some by the Israeli military.
Israel's subsequent assault on the Gaza Strip, later assessed to be a genocide by the United Nations and Holocaust scholars, has killed 74,000 Palestinians to date, with more than 22,000 children among them. Researchers with the Lancet Global Health Journal have said those figures are likely a severe undercount.
Trimm told Middle East Eye that industry professionals called her a "jihadist" and "antisemite", and warned her that she was putting people in danger through her advocacy.
"How is humanising Palestinian people being equated with antisemitism?" she said.

Gaza aid delay causes chronic shortage of medical supplies, WHO says
Getting humanitarian aid through Israel into Gaza is layered with "delay after delay", the World Health Organisation said Friday, as it decried "chronic shortages" of medical supplies.
Reinhilde Van de Weerdt, the WHO's representative in the Palestinian territories, said the health situation in the Gaza Strip "remains utterly dire", with none of its hospitals fully functional.
"Not enough humanitarian aid is entering Gaza, and definitely not enough to allow for a meaningful expansion and restoration of health services," she told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Jerusalem.
She said Israel's approval system for medical and other humanitarian supplies was proving a major bottleneck.
"It is laborious, time-consuming, with no guaranteed results," she said.
Based on the WHO's latest analysis, large volumes of medical supplies wait for clearance for a median of 74 days, said Van de Weerdt, adding that if it is not, "than we start that lengthy, cumbersome process all over again".
She added that the approval system kept changing, with new regulations introduced.
Van de Weerdt said standard health kits used worldwide had the lowest approval rate, while X-ray machines, sterilisation equipment and spare parts for CT scans and other essential machinery "get rejected regularly".
"In just the last six months alone, one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices was rejected four separate times," she said.
However, medicines move "relatively well", with almost 87 percent approved and one percent rejected, she added.
"It's not one single blockage. It's a system, layered with delay after delay... and on the other side of every one of these delays is a patient who is waiting," she said.
"We need the unimpeded and predicable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza, at scale.

Egyptian authorities have detained the entire newsroom of one of the country’s only independent media outlets in a move that rights groups have denounced as a “first” and an “alarming escalation” on free speech.
On 28 and 29 September, security forces raided the homes of the six journalists - Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel - who constitute the entire team working for Matsada2sh (Arabic for "Don’t believe").
The arrests bring the number of journalists detained in Egypt to 24.
"It is a first in Egypt: an entire newsroom behind bars," press freedom watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said, criticising the authorities for failing to reveal the journalists' whereabouts.
"It's a violation of the Egyptian Constitution, even though this is common practice. Journalists detained in Egypt are often forcibly disappeared for several days before being officially charged and brought before a court," the group added.

France approved 35 new sales of military equipment to Israel between May and September 2026, a new research by rights groups has found.
Jointly investigated by the Palestinian Youth Movement and the French collective Urgence Palestine, the probe documents shipments from French companies to Israel's military, including cooling systems for tanks and missile launchers, helmet visors for helicopter and fighter-jet pilots, connectors and electronic equipment, as well as surveillance systems.
"All were destined for Elbit Systems subsidiaries," the report, seen by Middle East Eye, indicates. Elbit Systems is a leading actor in the Israeli arms industry.
The findings, to be published next week, show that the equipment was manufactured across five regions in France by French companies, including the military conglomerate Thales, which produced and exported control panels used to operate weapons remotely.
These revelations come just months after the two organisations released a first joint investigation in April, which found that France exported more than 525 shipments of military-use equipment to Israel between October 2023 and March 2026.
The April report also documented 117 flights carrying F-35 fighter-jet components departing from Paris's main airport, Roissy-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).
In the new investigation, researchers identified four new suppliers and found that 33 of the 35 shipments passed through CDG airport, of which 32 were transported by Israel's national airline El Al.
